extracted.intended_audience: students and lovers of English literature; literary critics; translators; general educated readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for producing and judging English prose, translations, literary journals/thought-collections, and criticism — drawn from Pater's essays on prose style, translation, and criticism. Focuses on qualities of style, structure, rhythm, critical method, and what makes selections or 'thought' books effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical merits of prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Order, precision, directness are the radical merits of prose thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pater argues these qualities should form the criterion of prose style; within them a specific prose beauty arises. They are contrasted with poetic qualities and illustrated by reference to Dryden and later prose practice. Anti-pattern: prose invaded by poetic excess that sacrifices order and directness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable prose structure / architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose should conform, before all other aims, to laws of a structure primarily reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prose by its 'architecture' — clarity of organization and logical structure. Examples: Dryden and eighteenth-century correctness exemplify this; Elizabethan prose (too chaotic) fails it. Writers should test proposed 'prose-rhythm' rules against well-done examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose rhythm / technical metre for prose
rubrics_metrics.description: True prose rhythm can be taught by technical rules of metre, and these can be tested against good examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Saintsbury's suggested rules for prose rhythm are worth testing by applying them to established specimens; prose rhythm contributes materially to prose beauty. Guidance: compare rules to a wide survey of well-done English prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain distinction between prose and poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose must retain its indispensable qualities and not be invaded by the imaginative impulse of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning against 'unconscious blank verse' or poetic excess in prose (examples: some of Dickens, Carlyle). While poetry and prose share many qualities, their indispensable qualities differ; evaluators should look for order/precision in prose and beware lyricizing that undermines prose function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of style to matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Style should be related to the subject-matter; style cannot be judged entirely independently of what the writer has to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pater notes a tension: some treat style as independent (Saintsbury), others assert 'style is the man' — that style must suit the content. Evaluate whether the chosen style is appropriate and adequate for the writer's subject and personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eclectic aim: combine opposite excellences
rubrics_metrics.description: In a busy age aim at combining as many excellences as possible, even opposite ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given increased intellectual complexity, writers should seek an eclectic mix (e.g., correctness with imaginative range). This is a positive recommendation for producers and an evaluative standard for readers assessing modern style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, variety and directness (Steele)
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful essay/prose may exhibit transparency, variety, and directness; an 'unembarrassed matter' matched by an 'unembarrassed style.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Steele as example: truth to surface of common things, originality in effect, and a style that presents everyday life clearly. Evaluate essays on those virtues and on whether organization (grouping of short pieces) gives a connected, book-like character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth to the surface of common things
rubrics_metrics.description: Good prose shows truthfulness to everyday things and an original effect in rendering them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an author records manners/fashion/ordinary scenes with fidelity and originality (example: Steele's ramble). Anti-pattern: over-embellishing ordinary material so that its truth is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serenity and precision (Lamb)
rubrics_metrics.description: Serenity and precision are hallmarks of certain essayists (e.g., Charles Lamb), even when content touches deep feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humour and pathos for a maintained serenity and precise expression; good humour may also touch pity and awe without lapsing into lugubriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation: idiomatic quality and self-effacement
rubrics_metrics.description: A good translation should read like an original English work, be idiomatic and correct, and the translator must be willing to an act of self-denial or self-effacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mrs. Humphry Ward's translation of Amiel's Journal is praised for reading like excellent original English and for including an effective seventy-page prefatory essay. Translation guidance: blend fidelity with literary gift; provide useful introduc­tions/notes to contextualize the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal/'thoughts' volume usability
rubrics_metrics.description: A book of 'thoughts' should be one that may be fairly dipped into and yield good quotable sayings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate 'thought' collections on whether they provide memorable, independent aphorisms and whether the material rewards secondary reading; example: Amiel's Journal offers quotable passages suitable for dipping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature description must probe motive of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of nature are valuable when they accompany an intellectual effort to define the precise motive of the pleasure experienced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: mere scenic pleasure without reflective insight. Good example: Amiel's meditations on fog/frost that connect natural effect to moral or interior states; assess whether landscape writing reveals states of the soul or moral order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative criticism as constructive creation
rubrics_metrics.description: The best criticism is imaginative criticism: a constructive act that penetrates into the mind of the producer, shaping and recreating his work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pater holds that 'construction rests upon feeling, instinct, and ... will.' Evaluate criticism for its power of intellectual analysis, its imaginative reach, and whether it itself attains an aesthetic or constructive form rather than mere summary. Examples: Amiel's criticism of musical/compositional figures, Quinet, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable, convinced critical tone
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic should be fearlessly equitable and convinced that the subject is of real literary importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good criticism balances appreciation with intelligent limitation; it should make large exceptions skilfully and be animated by conviction of the subject's value. Anti-pattern: dismissive or merely pedantic criticism lacking breadth of appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism that makes literature enduring
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical writing should produce a powerful intellectual analysis in a form that helps make literature enduring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess critics on whether their analyses are shaped so as to clarify, preserve, and illuminate works for posterity — not merely transient judgments but constructs that aid lasting understanding (e.g., essays that prepare readers for study of Shakespeare).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guide readers toward the indisputable best
rubrics_metrics.description: A study or introduction should point readers to 'the best, the indisputable, rather than to the dubious portions' of an author's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing introductory criticism, aim to direct new readers to the most valuable parts of an oeuvre and to make seriatim divisions for special study; anti-pattern: overwhelming readers with undifferentiated selections that include marginal works without guidance.
